newsitem.title: FRANCE: Congo asks France to halt Brazzaville bloodshed.
newsitem.headline: Congo asks France to halt Brazzaville bloodshed.

text.p: Congo's ambassador to Paris said on Friday he had asked French parliamentarians to persuade their government to intervene in his country to prevent mutineers from toppling democratically-elected President Pascal Lissouba.

"It is clear that if France does not act as rapidly as possible, Congo's democratic regime will live or perish in bloodshed," envoy Pierre-Michel Nguimbi told the members of the French National Assembly in the letter released to the press.
Nguimbi asked the deputies to "intervene with the government to demand that it carry out a real policy of military help to save Congo from a very probable humanitarian and political disaster".

France has offered logistical support to a proposed peace force made up of African troops, but has refused to let its troops act as a buffer force between the forces of Lissouba and his enemy Denis Sassou Nguesso, Congo's Marxist leader for 13 years and his rival in presidential elections due in a month's time.
A 1,250-strong French military force pulled out of Congo after evacuating thousands of foreigners from fighting which is believed to have killed 1,000 to 3,000 people in Brazzaville since June 5.
A week-long ceasefire collapsed when Sassou launched his assault for the airport on Wednesday.
The Congolese envoy said France should intervene "in order to prevent more massacres in a region of Africa which in more than three years has seen hundreds of thousands die".
"No democracy can remain insensitive to the death of a young democratic republic, which has modelled itself on French political institutions," he said.
"Congo, with whom France has maintained a long relationship due to history and 40-year-old policy of cooperation, is despairing to see a friend abandon it," he wrote.

Meanwhile, U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun and Gabonese President Omar Bongo, who have been mediating the conflict, called on the international community to give their support to an African peacekeeping force for the capital Brazzaville.
"By not acting quickly, very quickly, there is the risk of seeing the chance to promote peace and democracy in Africa slip away," they wrote in the French daily Le Monde.
"Without logistical and financial support, necessary for sending, deploying and maintaining this African force in the Congo, the peace process is in danger of breaking down," they said.
"The moment is now or never to express solidarity with African countries who are trying to define a coherent policy in the face of conflict on the continents."
France said it was willing to provide the force with air transport.

"France is entirely ready to give its support in the form of air transport to the countries willing to participate in the force," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said at a daily news briefing.

He said Sahnoun would be in Paris later in the day to meet Foreign Minister Hubert Vedrine to discuss the matter and U.S. ambassador to Brazzavile Aubrey Hooks would meet Jean-Didier Roisin, the ministry's director of African affairs.
